facts.statement: The species Velocisaurus unicus was named and described by José Bonaparte in 1991.
facts.quote: In 1991 this dinosaur was described and named by José Bonaparte as Velocisaurus unicus.

facts.statement: Fossils of Velocisaurus were discovered in 1985 at Boca del Sapo in Neuquén province, Argentina, within the Santonian-aged Bajo de la Carpa Formation.
facts.quote: In 1985 Oscar de Ferrariis and Zulma Brandoni de Gasparini uncovered fossils at Boca del Sapo in Neuquén province of Patagonia from layers of the Bajo de la Carpa Formation, dating from the Santonian.

facts.statement: Velocisaurus was estimated to be about 1.5 meters long based on a 14 cm tibia.
facts.quote: Velocisaurus was probably around 1.5 m long, based on a tibia length of 14 cm.

facts.statement: Velocisaurus is the smallest known noasaurid dinosaur, second only to Berthasaura.
facts.quote: This makes it the smallest noasaurid, after Berthasaura.

facts.statement: Velocisaurus possessed a unique foot structure where the third metatarsal was the primary weight-bearing bone.
facts.quote: The foot is unique in that the middle (third) metatarsal has become the main weight-bearing element.

facts.statement: José Bonaparte interpreted the unique foot structure of Velocisaurus as an adaptation for a fast-running lifestyle.
facts.quote: Bonaparte explained it as an adaptation for a cursorial (running) lifestyle.

facts.statement: Bonaparte hypothesized that Velocisaurus was an omnivore because its fourth toe claw was straight rather than sharp.
facts.quote: Bonaparte suggested that Velocisaurus was itself an omnivore, as indicated by the fact that the sole claw found, of the fourth toe, was not trenchant but relatively straight.

facts.statement: Velocisaurus featured a long, slender tibia with a large flat distal end, resembling traits seen in coelurosaurs and ornithomimids.
facts.quote: A long and slender tibia with a large anteriorly flat distal end to accommodate a large ascending process of the astragalus (reminiscent of derived coelurosaurs and ornithomimids).

facts.statement: Velocisaurus had very thin, rod-like second and fourth metatarsals.
facts.quote: Very thin and rod-like metatarsals II and IV (metatarsal II is reduced to a lesser extent in other noasaurids and some abelisaurids as well).

facts.statement: José Bonaparte originally classified Velocisaurus in its own family, Velocisauridae.
facts.quote: Bonaparte originally assigned Velocisaurus to a family of its own, the Velocisauridae.

facts.statement: In 2004, the subfamily containing Velocisaurus was reclassified within the family Noasauridae and the superfamily Abelisauroidea.
facts.quote: In 2004 this subfamily was assigned to the Noasauridae within the more inclusive Abelisauroidea.

facts.statement: A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild found no signs of stress fractures in 12 examined foot bones of Velocisaurus.
facts.quote: In a 2001 study conducted by Bruce Rothschild and other paleontologists, 12 foot bones referred to Velocisaurus were examined for signs of stress fracture, but none were found.

facts.statement: Velocisaurus lived between 85.7 and 83.6 million years ago during the Santonian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Santonian to Santonian (85.7 to 83.6 million years ago)
